title: Dirk Willems turns back
hookLine: fleeing across ice, he turns to rescue his pursuer who fell through, and is captured

cards: The ice holds for the man running. It doesn't hold for the man chasing him. Winter, in a Dutch town called Asperen.
A prisoner has just escaped, knotting strips of cloth into a rope and letting himself down from a window. He runs for the frozen water and starts across, the officer sent to catch him close behind.
The prisoner makes it over. Then he hears the crack, the splash, and a man shouting for help from a hole in the ice. He's free.
Nobody would blame him for running. The man in the water was coming to take him back to die.

teach.b: Dirk's story comes to us through the Martyrs Mirror, a large book of Anabaptist martyr accounts. He had been arrested, the account says, for being baptized as a believer and letting others be baptized in his house.
Tradition says prison food had left him thin, and that's why the ice held him.
Then the pursuer fell through. And Dirk turned around, walked back across the ice he had just escaped over, and pulled the man out. What happened next is hard.
The pursuer, the account says, wanted to let him go.
But the town's burgomaster, standing on the bank, shouted at him to remember his oath. So the man Dirk had just saved took him back to prison. Dirk was condemned and burned.
Why turn back? The accounts don't give a speech. But Anabaptists like Dirk read the Sermon on the Mount as instructions, not ideals.

In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Paul puts it plainer: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him." Dirk's enemy wasn't hungry.
He was drowning. In Mennonite and Amish communities his story is told and retold, and people in other churches, and in none, tell it too. It doesn't ask anyone to go looking for martyrdom.
It asks a smaller, stranger question: when the one chasing you falls, what do you do?

how: Mennonite and Amish communities tell the story of Dirk Willems from the Martyrs Mirror, and an etching of him pulling his pursuer from the ice is a familiar image in Anabaptist homes and churches.

o: a jailer who helped a prisoner escape
a Dutch officer who fell through the ice
an Anabaptist who saved the man chasing him

games.q: Dirk Willems on the ice — tap the pairs.
p: held the runner, not the pursuer

s: Dirk escaped prison down a rope of knotted cloth
the account says he let himself down from a window and ran for the ice.
the man Dirk rescued let him go free
the pursuer wanted to, but the burgomaster shouted at him to remember his oath.
Dirk was caught because he slipped on the ice
he was already across. he turned back to pull his pursuer out.

games.q: you're Dirk. you've escaped across the ice. behind you, the officer sent to take you back falls through and cries for help. what do you do?
o: turn back and pull him out.
shout for someone else to help him, and keep going.
games.why: he turned back and saved him, and the man he saved took him back to prison. he was later burned.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's after you right now, not in danger, just pressing: a boss with a deadline, a critic, a relative with the same old complaint.

Ask not what would end the chase but what would help them, and choose one small thing, a finished task, a kind reply, a call back. If you pray, pray for that person by name; otherwise, hold them in mind without the usual defenses.

wordCard.voice: Dirk Willems. The Anabaptist who escaped across ice, then went back to save his drowning pursuer, and was captured for it.

carryVoice: Your line: he turned back. The ice had held for him, and he went back onto it. See you tomorrow.
